justification: This round's job was narrow and I treated it that way: re-fetch Microsoft Learn's 'Context Switches' page live and compare it sentence-by-sentence and structure-by-structure against the current 'What a context switch costs' section, because this exact spot survived round 1 (with a process-attributes list and the Chromium lift alongside it) and round 2 (alone, after the other two were genuinely fixed) as a three-item enumeration that mirrored the source's list order with near-synonym wording and a wrong nuance ('at least the same priority' narrowed to 'equal-priority'). I confirmed via `git diff e1a8ecc 05f4b95` that only three spots changed this round: this paragraph, the AutoResetEvent sentence, and the orders-of-magnitude sentence -- so I focused fresh scrutiny there and trusted round 2's already-reverified findings for everything else, spot-checking two of them myself anyway (below). The live Microsoft Learn page's 'most common reasons for a context switch' remains a flat three-bullet list in this order: (1) quantum expired and another thread with at least the same priority is ready, (2) a higher-priority thread has become ready, (3) a running thread needs to wait (and relinquishes the remainder of its time slice). The article's new paragraph no longer follows that shape. It leads with the source's third reason, recast as 'voluntary' (the thread blocks on a lock, signal or I/O completion and loses whatever was left of its slice), then groups the source's first two reasons under a single 'the scheduler taking the core away' banner and states them as a genuine two-condition test rather than two list items: quantum expiry is 'only a reason to switch if' a same-or-higher-priority thread is waiting, while a strictly-higher-priority thread's arrival ends a turn 'without waiting for its quantum to be spent at all'. Four checks specifically: (1) yes, it is organized differently -- a voluntary/involuntary split with an explicit necessary-condition ('only ... if') and contrastive ('while ... without') framing that the source's flat enumerative list does not have; this is a real structural transformation, not cosmetic reordering. (2) No invented examples beyond what the source's adjacent 'not ready threads' list already licenses (lock/signal/I/O-completion as reasons a thread waits); nothing fabricated. (3) The priority nuance is now stated correctly and distinctly from the round-2 error: 'at that priority or higher' correctly reconstructs the source's 'at least the same priority', and it is now explicitly contrasted with the separate, undiscounted case of a strictly-higher-priority thread -- exactly the distinction round 2 flagged as lost. (4) On the individual-clause question I looked hardest at this, because it's where the pattern fooled two prior rounds: clause-by-clause, 'a thread's quantum being spent is only a reason to switch if some other ready thread at that priority or higher is waiting for a turn' still maps onto the source's first bullet term-for-term (quantum expired/being spent, another thread/some other ready thread, at least the same priority/at that priority or higher, is ready/is waiting), and the higher-priority clause maps similarly onto the source's second bullet. What keeps this from being the same patchwriting round 2 flagged is that the source's bullets are asserted as flat parallel facts with no relationship between them, while the article recasts them as a necessary condition ('only ... if') paired with an explicit contrast ('without waiting for its quantum to be spent at all') that explains why the two are mechanistically different -- reasoning the source doesn't supply and the writer had to understand the mechanism to add. I judge this genuine synthesis rather than transcription, but the vocabulary overlap on those two clauses specifically is still close enough that I'm logging it as a minor finding rather than calling it fully clean; see below. I also independently re-fetched two other passages this round's diff did not touch, to keep my overall judgement fresh rather than inherited: the Chromium page (its actual quotable text is 'It's nearly impossible to build a rendering engine that never crashes or hangs' and 'Chromium uses multiple processes to protect the overall application from bugs and glitches' -- the article's 'a bug backlog to clear before shipping' phrase appears nowhere in the source, confirming round 2's finding still holds) and 'About Processes and Threads' (the article's container/what-runs-inside framing and its identity-vs-resource attribute regrouping still reorder the source's flat process-attribute list and use vocabulary -- 'container', 'who the process is to the rest of the system' -- absent from the source's plain enumeration). Both technical minors from round 2 are handled reasonably: the orders-of-magnitude sentence now gives the actual ratio ('about eight to twenty times') alongside 'roughly one order of magnitude', which is accurate for a ~7.7-20x jump, and states the thread-to-process step separately as 'two to three orders of magnitude', both defensible; the AutoResetEvent sentence now says each call 'operates on a native OS handle... because AutoResetEvent is a thin wrapper over one', which is closer to the suggested fix ('is backed by a native OS handle') than round 2's 'reaches into the kernel' framing, though it still implies a per-call kernel transition as a reasonable inference from the class's design rather than a claim the cited page states outright -- acceptable, not a new blocker. Nothing else in the article changed this round, and I found no new filler, padding, invented experience, mass-produced tics or dead-end links across a fresh read of the whole piece: the six programs are still distinct experiments with real, range-stated measurements, the two diagrams still have accessible title/desc, the four exercises are still varied (explain-a-mechanism, find-the-bug, measure-it, apply-a-decision), and the crosslinks scoping still explains the absence of links to unpublished sibling articles. Net: the round's one required job is genuinely, not cosmetically, done -- structure changed, nuance corrected, reasoning added -- which clears the blocker that held round 2 at 7.8; I'm not giving it a clean 9+ because two clauses inside the fixed passage still track the source's sentence-level vocabulary closely enough that one more pass of paraphrasing would remove all doubt.

issues.location: "What a context switch costs", second paragraph: "a thread's quantum being spent is only a reason to switch if some other ready thread at that priority *or higher* is waiting for a turn, while a strictly higher-priority thread becoming ready can end a running thread's turn without waiting for its quantum to be spent at all"
issues.problem: The paragraph's voluntary/involuntary restructuring and the added 'only ... if' / 'without waiting for its quantum' reasoning are genuine synthesis not present in Microsoft Learn's 'Context Switches' page, and the priority nuance is now stated correctly. But stripped of that framing, the two embedded clauses still map term-for-term onto the source's first two bullets ('quantum expired' / 'quantum being spent'; 'another thread with at least the same priority is ready' / 'some other ready thread at that priority or higher is waiting for a turn'; 'a thread with a higher priority has become ready to run' / 'a strictly higher-priority thread becoming ready'). This is not a blocker -- three rounds of independent critics would have caught a real reproduction, and this isn't one -- but it's close enough that a fourth pass, if one happens for other reasons, should finish the job by rewording those two clauses so they no longer parse as a synonym-substituted version of the source's two bullets even in isolation.
